text:
It seemed like the Chicago Bears were dodging bullet after bullet on the training camp injury front. Luther Burden III had a few scares, but the team reportedly feels good about his chances of being ready for the season opener. Cam Lewis was back on the practice field yesterday after some misfortune of his own. Ozzy Trapilo is somehow well on his way back to the field after rupturing his Achilles in January.

We even thought Ben Johnson's comments about Coby Bryant's reported 8-10 week timeline were a good sign for his future. However, it turns out we were all duped in that regard. Those comments were interpreted incorrectly, as Johnson announced that Bryant would instead be on the shelf for the next 4-6 months earlier today.

It's a true worst-case scenario for a Bears defense already down one key starter in nickelback Kyler Gordon. The injury will not only strain the secondary, but it'll also put a lot more pressure on the defensive line.

The Bears' front four has talent... but also many question marks

Virtually everyone expected the team to make a deeper nvestment in the defensive line this offseason. It was widely considered one of their most glaring weaknesses entering the offseason after failing to get consistent pressure on opposing QBs and often getting gouged in the running game last season.

However, the fact that they already have the league's fifth-most expensive defensive line limited how much they could justify improving the room in free agency. They instead opted for bargain-bin free agent additions and the sixth-round selection of Georgia Tech's Jordan van den Berg. It was always a bold strategy.

Fortunately, it was a bold strategy that appears to be off to a brilliant start. It's still far too early to have the rookie's gold jacket fitted for Canton, but there's no denying the fact that he's made serious waves at training camp. That's a good thing, too, because they desperately need some juice in the pass-rush department with Grady Jarrett not getting any younger and hope increasingly fading in Gervon Dexter getting any better in his fourth season.

Montez Sweat and Austin Booker's hopeful progression at least instills some hope on the edges, and they might be able to unlock last year's biggest free agent disappointment, Dayo Odeyingbo, on the interior. However, Sweat is the only sure thing in that regard, as well.

How long can the already injury-riddled secondary hold up?

The fact that the Bears signed Xavier Woods shortly after Bryant went down makes a lot more sense after Johnson's comments today. The veteran safety has 121 career starts under his belt, and he will at least provide some stability opposite rookie Dillon Thieneman.

Growing pains were always expected for Chicago's first-round selection, and that will especially be the case with Bryant out of action. While Woods has always been solid in coverage, Bryant is much more comfortable against the run than the veteran has been. That might be an area where they rely more on the rookie now, which could limit his upside and, in turn, remove the alignment flexibility that Dennis Allen was clearly vying for with the team's new safety duo.

It's also fair to question how well the new-look secondary will gel after losing one of their best players until (at least) December. The importance of getting Kyler Gordon back in the lineup has never been more paramount. Unfortunately, his health has always been far from reliable.

The loss the secondary suffered today cannot be understated, and it's going to have a wide-ranging impact on the entire defense.

"I'm not really sure what the issue was, but nobody ran up to me in a panic," Stafford said. "I don't think it was anything too major."

After weeks of split reps, film study, and heavy debate, the Minnesota Vikings have made their decision at quarterback. Head coach Kevin O’Connell is rolling with Kyler Murray over J.J. McCarthy this season, the team announced Tuesday.

Murray signed a league-minimum deal with the Vikings this offseason and every indication suggested he would eventually win the job. The team was desperate for stability at the position after a year that saw McCarthy, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer all take snaps under center.

Vikings name Kyler Murray starting QB, Is this the right decision?

Not only did Murray’s Arizona Cardinals tenure end abruptly, but his lack of production in recent seasons was hard to ignore. With O’Connell’s strong reputation as a quarterback whisperer, Murray signing with the Vikings felt like the ultimate opportunity to potentially reignite his career.

In seven NFL seasons, Murray has never reached the 4,000-yard mark and has thrown 25 passing touchdowns only once. O’Connell’s system is built to elevate passing numbers; just ask Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold, who both hit those benchmarks under his watch.

Now that the dust has settled on the competition, all eyes turn to McCarthy. Entering his third season, the former national champion finds himself on the bench, now leaving his long-term future in Minnesota suddenly up in the air.

San Francisco 49ers pass rusher Nick Bosa hasn’t played since week three of last season after suffering a torn ACL in his right knee. He’s been working on his recovery all offseason, but hit a setback this week after head coach Kyle Shanahan revealed he’s dealing with tendinitis.

Shanahan and the rest of the coaching staff don’t appear concerned, as they described it as "a pretty normal thing with ACLs."

Still no firm timetable for Bosa's return, but Shanahan gave an update Monday saying that Bosa is currently week-to-week with tendinitis. He also said he has "no concerns" about Bosa's long-term status and expects him ready for the Week 1 opener against the Los Angeles Rams.

title: Injury to Nate Wiggins marred another strong practice by Ravens' defense - The Athletic
description:
— It started as a great rep for Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins.
He stayed stride-for-stride with rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane, who has been punishing Ravens cornerbacks throughout training camp.
Members of the Ravens’ athletic training staff tended to him immediately and helped him onto a medical cart nearby.
His form early in training camp suggested that was a realistic possibility.
• Nose tackle Travis Jones was activated from the PUP list and made his training camp debut Tuesday.
text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — It started as a great rep for Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins. He stayed stride-for-stride with rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane, who has been punishing Ravens cornerbacks throughout training camp. Wiggins had good position on Lane as they moved toward the end zone. The cornerback then found the slightly overthrown football and attempted to make a play on it.

In the process, Wiggins appeared to take an awkward step and tumbled to the ground. He immediately grabbed his left leg and started writhing in pain. Members of the Ravens’ athletic training staff tended to him immediately and helped him onto a medical cart nearby. After arriving outside the training room, Wiggins was helped off the cart and was unable to put any weight on his left leg.

The potential of a significant injury to one of the team’s most important players marred the Ravens’ 11th training camp practice and provided first-year head coach Jesse Minter with some early adversity as he heads into what Baltimore hopes will be a quick turnaround for a traditionally strong defense that struggled mightily last season.

“We don’t have a ton of information on that yet,” Minter said following the practice. “We’ll kind of get it looked at and see where it’s at.”

After Wiggins’ MRI, the Ravens believe the 22-year-old cornerback avoided a major injury, per a team source. He could be sidelined for a bit, but the expectation is that the first-round pick from 2024 will be back sooner rather than later.

Ravens players and decision-makers were certainly concerned on the field. Several players, including quarterback Lamar Jackson, consoled Wiggins after he was loaded onto the cart. Head athletic trainer Adrian Dixon, who had been with Wiggins, returned to the field to speak with general manager Eric DeCosta, and Minter came over to briefly join the conversation.

“Really not much between the two guys in the play, so whether it was hitting the ground or whatever it was, we’ll see what it looks like,” Minter said.

The Ravens do have some depth at cornerback. Marlon Humphrey is a four-time Pro Bowler, and the team is optimistic that he’ll rebound after a difficult 2025 season. The Ravens re-signed veteran Chidobe Awuzie, who has made 86 career starts and played well last year. T.J. Tampa, a 2024 fourth-round pick, is having a great camp and was already pushing for a more prominent role. There are a number of talented young corners behind them, including Keyon Martin, Bilhal Kone and rookie fifth-round pick Chandler Rivers.

Still, although he has fought some inconsistencies through his first two NFL seasons, Wiggins is the Ravens’ closest answer to a matchup cornerback. Any plan to play more man-to-man defense this year and be more aggressive at the line of scrimmage hinged partly on Wiggins being on the field and having a breakout season. His form early in training camp suggested that was a realistic possibility.

“Nate Wiggins is a high-caliber, first-round pick corner — a great player,” Minter said. “You’re not just going to say, ‘Oh, everything’s the same,’ whatever, because it’s built around the talents of the players. I just know that we’ll be able to do things, however it shakes out. I feel good about the secondary.”

It’s a tough development, though, for Wiggins. He had groin surgery this offseason, and he remarked that he felt fully healthy for the first time in his young career. It took just three weeks for that to change.

Jackson won’t play Saturday

The Ravens will open the preseason Saturday night at M&T Bank Stadium against the Philadelphia Eagles. Minter confirmed that many of the team’s more “established players,” including Jackson, will not play. Jackson has not played in a preseason game since the 2021 matchup against Washington at FedEx Field, when running back J.K. Dobbins tore up a knee.

“It’s an individual basis,” Minter said. “I would say, based on maybe some of the experience and how many snaps they’ve played and things like that. I do think there’s value. We will have three joint practices, which I view in high regard for the work that we’ll be able to get there in a more controlled environment for specific positions, especially. So, it’s a little bit of an individual basis, for sure.”

Other camp notes

• Wide receiver Zay Flowers returned to the field Tuesday after missing just one practice with a quad contusion. Flowers did individual drills and headed inside about an hour into the practice. Martin and defensive tackle Aeneas Peebles also returned to the field after missing time recently. The list of non-participants in Tuesday’s practice included quarterback Skylar Thompson, running back Rasheen Ali, wide receivers Rashod Bateman and Dayton Wade, inside linebackers Teddye Buchanan (on the physically unable to perform list) and Carl Jones, and safety Jahquez Robinson.

• Nose tackle Travis Jones was activated from the PUP list and made his training camp debut Tuesday. Travis Jones has been working his way back from pectoral surgery. “Travis looks great,” Minter said. “He’ll be a guy that in the first few days we’ll probably have to hold him back, which is sometimes a good thing. But, ‘Trav’ looks amazing striking the sled. He’s been putting in a ton of work off the field, in the weight room, conditioning. I expect big, big things.”

• Rookie seventh-round defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny, who is trying to win a reserve job, left practice early after getting banged up during the team session. He walked slowly off the field and then stayed under one of the medical tents along the sideline for a while. He then walked inside with a member of the athletic training staff.

• Offensive lineman Emery Jones Jr. drove inside linebacker Jay Higgins IV to the ground, and the two got tangled up and exchanged shoves before order was quickly restored. Emery Jones has been ornery at times in practice, and Higgins felt the brunt of it.

• Undrafted safety Silas Walters picked off an overthrown ball by Joe Fagnano. Humphrey, who has strung together a couple of solid practices, also intercepted Jackson on a ball intended for Mark Andrews in the end zone. Overall, it was another day where Baltimore’s defense dominated the offense.

• The offensive highlights included a few big plays to Devontez Walker and Cornelius Johnson, who has struggled at times with drops, laying out to make a sparkling touchdown catch of a Tyler Huntley pass.

• Kicker Tyler Loop had another really good day, making all seven of his field goal attempts. He also remained perfect from beyond 50 yards. After how last season ended, Loop will ultimately be judged by how he performs in the regular season, particularly in the clutch. However, he’s doing everything he can to quiet some of the outside sentiment that the Ravens need to bring in another kicker. He didn’t kick the ball particularly well at the team’s stadium practice in College Park, Md., on Aug. 2. Otherwise, he’s been close to flawless.

The San Francisco 49ers were destroyed by injuries last year, and one of the most impactful was the loss of defensive end Nick Bosa, who suffered a season-ending ACL tear just three weeks into their 2025 campaign.

With the five-time Pro Bowler having surgery in the middle of the season, he started training camp off without an injury designation, as the team eased him back into practice. However, he's missed recent sessions due to soreness.

Advertisement

49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke to the media on Tuesday and revealed that Bosa has tendinitis in the knee that he had surgery on this offseason, which is what has kept him off the field. Shanahan said that Bosa is week-to-week at this point.

This is rough news, as Bosa has had three ACL surgeries in his life, and just a couple of weeks ago, he told the MMQB's Albert Breer that they cleaned up some tendinitis that he had in that knee during the surgery this offseason. Bosa believed that once he was fully done with rehab and going full speed, his knee would actually feel better than before this last tear.

San Francisco has an aging roster, and they need to get the most out of their best players in 2026 if they want to accomplish their goals before their window slams shut. Bosa is near the top of that list.

Raiders WR Dont’e Thornton (undisclosed) missed his fourth straight practice Wednesday.

Thornton was at practice in street clothes Tuesday, missing his fourth straight. He left a training camp practice early last week and has not received a diagnosis or return timetable. Jack Bech, Jalen Nailor, and Tre Tucker are listed as the Raiders’ starting wide receivers on the team’s first unofficial depth chart of the preseason. Seahawks placed FB Robbie Ouzts (neck) on injured reserve.

He dealt with a neck injury heading into the Super Bowl and will now head to injured reserve due to another neck issue. text:
Los Angeles Rams star receiver Puka Nacua left practice early with team trainer Reggie Scott on Tuesday, Aug. 11, according to multiple reports. Head coach Sean McVay told reporters he had no update and wasn't sure of the reason for Nacua's early exit.

The Rams were in the middle of a joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys ahead of Saturday's preseason opener against the Kansas City Chiefs.

Nacua, 25, is entering his fourth NFL season and coming off a banner year in which he led the league with 129 receptions for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns and was named first team All-Pro for the first time in his career.

His offseason, however, has been marred by controversy.

Nacua was accused of biting a woman and making antisemitic remarks during a dinner on New Year's Eve, according to a civil lawsuit filed in March. Through his attorney, Nacua denied the allegations "in the strongest possible terms."

His attorney announced on April 1 that Nacua had entered rehab. McVay told USA TODAY Sports on April 21 that Nacua had completed his rehab.

ESPN's Adam Schefter reported earlier on Aug. 11 that Nacua could still face a suspension by the NFL.

For now, though, the Rams are hoping for good news on their star receiver's health.

Matthew Stafford reacts to Puka Nacua injury

Stafford, the NFL's reigning MVP, told ESPN's Lindsey Thiry that while he didn't see what happened to Nacua, he's hopeful about his WR1.

"I'm not really sure what the issue was, but nobody ran up to me in a panic," Stafford said. "So I don't think it was anything too major."

Puka Nacua injury update

It appears Nacua is dealing with a minor injury.

NFL Media's Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday evening that Nacua was "dealing with minor soreness in his groin" and that the Rams are "just being cautious."

This story has been updated with new information.

text:
PHILADELPHIA -- Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio suggested outside linebacker Jonathan Greenard still has a ways to go in his recovery from a pec injury.

"We ain't going to see him for another couple weeks, at least," Fangio said Tuesday.

Greenard was placed on the physically unable to perform list in late July after suffering what the team described as a pec strain while lifting before camp.

The Eagles relayed at the time that this was not a long-term injury. Fangio, though, previously cast some doubt on whether Greenard would be able to practice with the team before the start of the regular season, saying "that remains to be seen."

Philadelphia acquired Greenard, 29, in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings during draft weekend in April and agreed to a lucrative new deal with the star linebacker.

The Eagles sent two third-round draft picks -- the No. 98 pick in this year's draft and a third-rounder next year -- to the Vikings for Greenard, who then agreed to a four-year, $100 million extension that also includes $50 million in guaranteed money.

Greenard is expected to assume a starting role for the Super Bowl-hopeful Eagles, leading a group that also includes Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith Jr., AJ Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie. Hunt in particular has enjoyed a strong summer.

Greenard had three sacks in 12 games last season after a pair of double-digit sack campaigns the previous two years in Minnesota.

text:
Attendance

Physically Unable to Perform — OL Nick Gargiulo (knee)

Injured reserve — DL Matt Henningsen (Achilles)

Did not practice — WR Jaylen Waddle (muscle strain), WR Marvin Mims Jr. (groin), WR Michael Bandy, C Luke Wattenberg (shoulder), C Alex Forsyth, TE Caleb Lohner (foot/ankle), OLB Dasan McCullough.

Left practice — C Michael Deiter

The Broncos are running low on healthy centers

Eventually, the Broncos expect to have one of the best offensive lines in the NFL with all five starters back for a third year together.

Regardless of how many snaps the other starters play Friday in Atlanta, who is snapping the ball could be a storyline to follow after another depth center went down with an injury Tuesday. Michael Dieter was injured during a running play. The Broncos’ training staff examined his right leg before he needed help onto a cart to exit the practice field.

Dieter is the third center to sustain an injury during camp. The team’s starter, Luke Wattenberg, sustained a shoulder injury early last week. He’s been in pads the past couple of days but has not participated beyond stretching.

“We’ll work through it,” Broncos coach Sean Payton said. “We have guys that are flexible. We’ll be fine.”

Alex Forsyth has missed the past two days, elevating Dieter to the No. 1 spot. The next man up with Denver’s top three options at center unavailable was rookie undrafted free agent Gavin Ortega. Veteran backup lineman Calvin Throckmorton also took some snaps with quarterback Bo Nix.

Another potential option is all-Pro guard Quinn Meinerz, who took some reps at center earlier in his pro career. Meinerz did some snapping between practice periods Tuesday but did not get any actual reps at the position.

“I sharpen that tool every single year just in case,” Meinerz said. “I’ve got to have it in the back pocket. I know that it’s important to add that value to the offensive line room in an emergency situation. Even last year against the Chargers at the end of the year, I was technically one snap away from having to go play some center.”

Payton seemed to downplay turning to Meinerz, noting his team still has enough options before him. Meinerz said former Broncos offensive line coach Mike Munchak moved him to center at times during his rookie year in 2020 after he spent a couple of days at Senior Bowl practices getting some reps at the position.

While Meinerz never saw himself as a potential center, that experiment has helped his evolution into one of the NFL’s best guards.

“I learn the offense consistently from a center’s perspective,” Meinerz said. “I think you, as a guard, if you can understand our scheme from a center’s perspective, it will allow you to identify the defense quicker. If a new center comes in, like a younger guy or someone that’s played guard and center, I can help them identify the ‘Mike’ (linebacker) and stuff like that. It’s a tool I constantly keep sharpened, just in case it’s needed. I hope I don’t have to use that tool, but if I do, I’m ready.”

Pat Bryant’s impressive camp continues

While new No. 1 wide receiver Jaylen Waddle continues to miss time with a muscle strain, second-year wideout Pat Bryant continued to be one of the stars of this camp Tuesday. He went up high over a defender to haul in a touchdown pass from Nix on a fourth-down play during a best-on-best team period, much to the delight of the fans in attendance — and his teammates.

“Pat Bryant, man, he’s a guy who literally can do everything on the field,” Broncos star linebacker Nik Bonitto said. “I mean, you see it — he’s making amazing play after amazing play every day. He’s out here and just his route running, all the things he does for the offense. He’s going to be a player for sure.”

Undrafted rookie wideout Kolbe Kastis also had an acrobatic touchdown catch on a pass from Sam Ehlinger late in practice during a two-minute drill.

Thumbs up

Under the radar? It’s not often a player with 104 targets to his name in the previous season flies under the radar, but that might be happening a bit with Troy Franklin. The third-year wide receiver hasn’t made the laundry list of highlight-reel grabs that Bryant has, but he’s been steady in camp. It’s not going to be easy for anybody to carve out a big role in the passing game behind Waddle, Sutton and maybe Bryant, but Franklin’s come a long way from his rookie year in 2024 in terms of understanding the offense and the ability to play multiple positions.

Thumbs down

Leave that one in the bag … During one situational period, the No. 1 offense faced a fourth down from the 22-yard line with seconds remaining and down six points. Nix ended up rolling to his right and tried to force a ball to a double-covered R.J. Harvey near the front-right corner of the end zone. It fell incomplete. If the Broncos face a similar scenario in a game, expect them to try something else.

Odds and ends

* The past couple of practices have focused pretty heavily on specific situations during team scrimmage periods. It’s been a staple for Payton-coached teams. The Broncos went 11-2 in one-score games in 2025, tying an NFL record for most one-score wins and playing a huge role in the team’s ability to both win the AFC West and land the No. 1 seed in the playoffs.

“Well, the situational part of the game, there’s like 53 — a lot of them are two-minute related — that come up each week,” Payton said. “It’s knowing how to react, knowing how to react defensively to what they’re thinking, offensively to what we’re thinking. You want to get to a point where you know them cold.”

* Bonitto has improved his sack total each year since entering the league, and has finished in the top-10 of the defensive player of the year each of the past two seasons. He has 27.5 sacks over the past two years. One of the resources at his disposal that has helped fuel his ascension? The guy he faces in practice, left tackle Garett Bolles.

“He’s been in this league for so long, and he’s gone against so many different types of rushers,” Bonitto said. “He’s probably, in my opinion, the best as a pass blocker in the game for sure. I’m always trying to just pick his brain about things, and what can help me in my game, and just how I can take that next step as a rusher to improve myself.”

* The Broncos opened the week with a pair of long practices in pads — “two bangers in a row,” All-Pro guard Quinn Meinerz told The Post — and now will transition to preparing for their preseason opener at Atlanta, which is Friday. Wednesday’s practice, originally slated to be open to the public, is instead closed and will be more of a game-planning session. Or at least as much of one as happens in the preseason. “It’ll be a couple evenings, call it two practices and maybe a walkthrough. Again, the most important thing is just getting the proper evaluation on (your own) guys.”

title: Dodgers' Dalton Rushing doesn't believe he needs surgery for UCL injury - The Athletic
authors: Fabian Ardaya, Katie Woo and Jeshua Kidd
description:
In rehashing the injury for the first time publicly, Rushing said the tear was not a massive surprise — or an area of real immediate concern.
It’s not the setup anyone envisioned, but it’s the catching situation the Dodgers are stuck with until Will Smith returns from injury.
Rushing had served as the Dodgers’ primary catcher ever since Smith hit the injured list in June with an inflamed disc in his neck.
The Dodgers still see Rushing filling a potential role, even if he cannot catch.
That has been more than enough for the Dodgers to want to keep Rushing as a viable option.
text:
LOS ANGELES — Dalton Rushing said his season is not over yet. The Los Angeles Dodgers backstop told The Athletic he does not believe he will need surgery to address a slight tear in the ulnar collateral ligament in his throwing elbow.

“I don’t have to go lay on a table and get my arm cut open,” Rushing said after the Dodgers’ 6-5 win over Kansas City on Monday night. “That’s a good thing. That’s where we’re at right now.”

Rushing felt discomfort while warming up before a game against the Boston Red Sox on Aug. 2 and was a late scratch from the lineup before being placed on the injured list a day later. In rehashing the injury for the first time publicly, Rushing said the tear was not a massive surprise — or an area of real immediate concern.

“From a structural standpoint, we had a history a little bit of it,” Rushing said. “(The Dodgers) were aware of it. Everyone was aware of it. I think that’s what popped up as of recently on scans and kind of threw up a red flag for some people.

“But as far as the feel of it, we’re worried about the muscle side of it that surrounds it. That’s what we’re going to rehab.”

Doctors, Rushing said, are “not worried about anything structurally right now” in his elbow, which fuels his hope to avoid a season-ending surgery. The Dodgers are still hopeful their former top prospect could provide a boost in their quest for a third consecutive World Series title.

Manager Dave Roberts said last week there is a “very small” chance that Rushing catches again this season, though much of the Dodgers’ evaluation will depend on the results of scans after Rushing goes four to six weeks without throwing.

“I hope I’m wrong,” Roberts said at the time after downplaying the odds.

The Dodgers already have contingencies. They spent the day after Rushing complained of symptoms trading for a pair of catchers they knew previously in Ben Rortvedt and Hunter Feduccia to help address the position. It’s not the setup anyone envisioned, but it’s the catching situation the Dodgers are stuck with until Will Smith returns from injury.

Rushing had served as the Dodgers’ primary catcher ever since Smith hit the injured list in June with an inflamed disc in his neck. Smith is expected to take batting practice on the field this week for the first time since his injury, Roberts said on Monday.

“This is going to be a big week for Will,” Roberts said.

If all goes well, Smith is expected to be behind the plate in October. The Dodgers still see Rushing filling a potential role, even if he cannot catch.

Rushing has continued to swing in the week since going on the injured list, wearing protective gear on his right elbow. The Dodgers have a clear need for a left-handed bat as they roll with what on most nights is exclusively a right-handed bench. That unbalanced roster construction has complicated things, Roberts said Monday afternoon, as the Dodgers have clear redundancies. Roberts said he will start Alex Call on Tuesday, which will mark the outfielder’s first start since July 21 and just his seventh game overall in that span.

“It’s not ideal,” Roberts said.

Rostering Rushing is not a clear-cut solution if he medically cannot play a position (and the Dodgers famously employ Shohei Ohtani as a designated hitter), but they’re keeping the possibility alive.

The 25-year-old has put up an .809 OPS in 245 plate appearances so far this season, ranking as the fifth-most productive offensive player at the catcher position in that much playing time. That has been more than enough for the Dodgers to want to keep Rushing as a viable option. It’s also a chance for the team to continue making the most of what has been a strong first full season in the big leagues for Rushing.

“It’s just adversity,” Rushing said of the path ahead.

text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- Chicago Bears safety Coby Bryant will be out four to six months after undergoing knee surgery, coach Ben Johnson announced Tuesday.

Bryant had surgery Aug. 7, four days after he hyperextended his left knee and sustained a bone bruise and small fracture, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. The safety was injured during one-on-ones and was driven back to the building on a cart.

"He's gonna be in a hurry to get back to help us out there at the end of the year," Johnson said.

According to Johnson, the Bears sought multiple opinions on Bryant's injury, which led the safety to need surgery.

Bryant's extended absence delivers a significant blow to the Chicago secondary, which has dealt with a rash of injuries throughout training camp. Cornerback Kyler Gordon has been on the physically unable to perform list with a calf injury since before the start of practices after experiencing a "delay" in his recovery, according to general manager Ryan Poles. Backup safety Elijah Hicks is also on the PUP list with a calf injury, and the Bears lost reserve defensive backs Gervarrius Owens and Dallis Flowers to significant leg injuries last week.

Cam Lewis, who was filling in at nickel corner before moving to safety in Bryant's absence, got injured during Saturday's practice and missed the next day's session. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said he did not think Lewis' injury would be long term but was not aware of a timeline for his return.

The Bears signed 10-year veteran safety Xavier Woods on Friday to mitigate the absences. Woods played opposite first-round rookie Dillon Thieneman during Sunday's practice with the first-team defense and figures to solidify that spot amid the absences of Bryant and Lewis.

Bryant was Chicago's marquee free agent acquisition, having signed a three-year, $40 million contract as the Bears turned over their safety unit this offseason. Bryant and Thieneman were brought in to replace safeties Kevin Byard (signed with New England Patriots) and Jaquan Brisker (signed with Pittsburgh Steelers), who were a part of a defense that ranked No. 1 in the NFL with 33 takeaways.

Johnson provided two additional injury updates Tuesday. Wide receiver Luther Burden III, who has a groin injury, will "hopefully" be ready for the start of the season when the Bears open at Carolina on Sept. 12.

Left tackle Ozzy Trapilo, who ruptured his patellar tendon during the playoffs, could return from the PUP list by the end of training camp, per Johnson.

"He's hitting his hurdles ... and he's doing a good job," Johnson said.

text:
If it were solely up to Rashawn Slater, he would be getting every rep in practice right now.

But since the Chargers left tackle is returning from a serious knee injury, the two-time Pro Bowler knows he needs to take a cautious approach at times in order to be ready for Week 1.

"It's definitely a struggle sometimes. Just want to be out there for the team," Slater said Tuesday. "I hate missing out, but one of the really good things about our [medical] staff is they're so thoughtful and they understand in some ways they need to protect players from themselves a little bit

"It's difficult, but at the same time, when you compare it to what's to come, it's not so difficult of a decision," Slater added.

To recap, Slater suffered a torn patellar tendon on August 7 of training camp in 2025, an injury that caused him to miss the entire season.

He participated in the Bolts offseason program and was cleared for training camp, although he did take some teams reps off here and there in the first week of camp.

Slater said Tuesday that he had a "little" flare up in his knee last week in San Diego, prompting a consultation with the medical staff.

He was then out there Wednesday and Thursday but has missed the past four practices, although the 27-year-old added Tuesday that he's not worried about where he's at right now.

"Nothing crazy, just being thoughtful and learning," Slater said. "I mean, you have a surgery like that, the rehab went great but things can still happen and things are different. Really, we're just learning.

"This is my first time playing football in a year, so there's going to be things that are different. We have to be mindful about them," Slater added. "But again, nothing that's concerning, just got to keep going, keep being thoughtful. Getting ready for what matters."

Slater later summed up the approach the Bolts are taking in a plain and simple manner.

"We're not putting you in Bubble Wrap, but we also need to respect the fact this is a significant thing to come back from," Slater said.

As far as Slater's return to the field, he said he's feeling great.

And when asked if his knee feels different from before the injury, Slater admitted it does ... but in a good way.

"It does feel different, it feels better, honestly," Slater said. "I can get in my stance with no pain ... it feels really good, really positive when I'm moving.

"It's strong, it's stable. Obviously, when you do a procedure, there's some things that changed slightly. There's more tissue in the knee," Slater added. "The repair is really strong, so because of that there's extra tissue and stuff. Does that change the mechanics? Not that I notice. Just taking it day by day. It's going well."

As Slater works toward being ready for the regular season, he's also getting adjusted to Mike McDaniel's new offensive scheme and a new offensive line coach in Butch Barry.

"Coach Barry, I think he's a great coach. I think a lot of our beliefs about O-Line play are very similar. He's a big fan of a lot of the techniques I have always pride myself on," Slater said. "It's fun to be able to play for him and learn from him. I think we have some really fun stuff. It feels good to lean on the stuff that I feel most comfortable doing, too."

He later added of McDaniel: "He gets a lot of credit for his scheme ... but just like Butch, he's more about how you do things than what you're doing. All that matters of course, but at the end of the day, he sees it as the mentality and approach you have to take to practice every day is what's most important. I like that a lot."

And, a dozen practices into camp, there is still a left guard battle raging on next to Slater's spot at left tackle.

While Slater said he might usually prefer to get ample reps next to the left guard, the fact that everyone is in a new system changes that mindset a bit.

"We're all new to this scheme, per se, so some of the techniques and stuff, we're all learning together," Slater said. "I think that helps a little bit because we're all starting off on the same page."

When healthy, Slater has been among the NFL's best players at his posiiton.

That was true in 2024 when he posted an overall Pro Football Focus grade of 91.1, a mark that ranked second among all offensive tackles.

He also posted a 90.4 pass-blocking grade, which ranked third among tackles. And his 82.8 run-blocking grade ranked fifth among players in his position group.

And if we look at the 2021, 2023 and 2024 seasons — when Slater has played at least 15 games — he's been an elite player.

His overall PFF grade in those three seasons is 89.6, which ranks 20th among all players with at least 2,400 snaps. That mark is seventh among all offensive linemen and is fifth among tackles.

So, while it may be frustrating for Slater to miss some practice time now, the whole goal is for him to be ready to roll for Week 1 against the Cardinals when he can resume his place among the NFL's best left tackles.

"Just controlling what I can control, doing everything I can and staying locked in mentally and physically, too," Slater said. "I know it's coming and when that happens, we're not going to be worried about this. I just keep that in mind and trust the process."

He later added: "I feel like the real celebration is going to be when I'm out there playing again on Sundays."

text:
Baltimore Ravens cornerback and 2024 first-round draft pick Nate Wiggins was carted off the field roughly an hour into Tuesday’s practice after suffering a left leg injury.

Wiggins tangled with rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane during one-on-one drills and fell to the turf. He appeared unable to put weight on the leg as he entered the team facility.

Asked about the potential seriousness of the injury, first-year head coach Jesse Minter said Wiggins was still being evaluated.

"Not a whole lot," Minter responded. "I think there’s optimism, but again, we’ll look at it, we’ll see where it’s at. It’s one of those plays, really not much between the two guys in the play. So whether it was hitting the ground or whatever it was, we’ll see what it looks like."

Wiggins’ injury comes two practices after two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers left Friday’s session with a thigh bruise. Flowers returned to limited action Tuesday after missing Sunday's practice.

Wiggins started all 17 games and had three interceptions in his second season in 2025 after the Ravens selected him 30th overall in the 2024 draft out of Clemson.

He comes into the season as the starter on the left side and perhaps the team’s top cornerback, even in front of four-time Pro Bowler Marlon Humphrey, who has transitioned into a slightly different role.

The Ravens made minimal upgrades at the position this offseason despite finishing 2025 tying for the NFL’s second-worst pass defense.

"I got a lot of confidence in the corner room," Minter said. "I look at Marlon probably at his best couple days the last couple times out here. (Chidobie Awuzie), I mean, this guy’s played a ton of football, played at a really high level. I think he’s had a great camp up to this point. T.J. Tampa has done a lot of great things. Keyon Martin has done a lot of good stuff. Chandler (Rivers) has done a lot of great stuff."

Minter also confirmed that quarterback Lamar Jackson and other regulars won’t play during Saturday night’s home preseason opener against the Philadelphia Eagles, but insisted there’s still value in preseason games.

"Every year that I’ve been associated with the NFL, there’s a guy in the first preseason game that you might not have real high expectations for, and then they go out in the game and play at a different level than maybe they practiced," Minter said. "And so that’s what you want to see. You want to see guys take advantage of the opportunity, make plays."

text:
Every practice is critical for the Seattle Seahawks during training camp. Some role players get the chance to elevate themselves in the depth chart and get more chances on the field. Wide receiver Jake Bobo entered training camp feeling great after a new contract with the Seahawks. His momentum fell short early during training camp as he suffered a hamstring injury.

On Monday, Bobo returned to the field after nearly two weeks, but not without some development with the team. He returns to the team with his regular spot, but with some changes elsewhere.

Jake Bobo’s Roster Spot Should Be Fine

Usually, when a non-starter is out for nearly two weeks during training camp, their spot on the 53-man roster is in trouble. With Bobo and the Seahawks, however, there is an understanding that he is more valuable than his regular-season stats from last year. He is among the wide receivers who spent the most time on the Seahawks’ roster. Bobo is entering his fourth season in the league, all of them in Seattle.

Bobo has caught 34 receptions for 323 yards and three touchdowns in his three years. He has, however, played in 45 games and made three starts. He made a pivotal 17-yard touchdown catch in the NFC Championship win over the Los Angeles Rams. This was easily the biggest play in his career.

Ultimately, he is one of the best run blockers from the receiver corps. He also provides great effort and knowledge to the Seahawks’ offense. Even with a new offensive coordinator in Brian Fleury, Bobo feels comfortable with the offensive schemes and how he is best utilized. There could be potential big moment games where he might be the top receiver. Regardless, he is one of the heart and souls of the receiver corps. He isn’t going anywhere.

Some Changes at the Wide Receiver Position

Bobo’s absence did, however, open some room for a possible seventh receiver spot to be addressed. With him out, this allowed second-year draft pick Ricky White III, veteran Cody White, formerly undrafted second-year Montrorie Foster Jr. and rookie Emmanuel Henderson to take advantage of the extra reps in practices. Both Cody and Ricky White spent some time on the Seahawks’ roster last season.

title: Falcons training camp takeaways: Checking on quarterback, the offensive line and more
description:
The Atlanta Falcons are about two weeks into training camp, and that seemed like a good time for me to share my most pertinent thoughts.
Quarterback questions I tried to come up with a sunnier way to say this, but quarterback is a mess at the moment.
Rush and Strand split reps with the second team in 11-on-11 work during Saturday night’s practice at Lanier High School.

He’s still not with the team due to an issue Stefanski said the team is “working through.”
text:
The Atlanta Falcons are about two weeks into training camp, and that seemed like a good time for me to share my most pertinent thoughts. Let’s dive in.

Quarterback questions

I tried to come up with a sunnier way to say this, but quarterback is a mess at the moment. Tua Tagovailoa is coming off one of his worst professional seasons and was limited for the first seven practices by back tightness he began experiencing for the first time in his career shortly before training camp. You can’t question Tagovailoa’s toughness. In his career, he has had a high ankle sprain that required surgery, a hip dislocation that also required surgery and multiple concussions. He’s the strong favorite to start Week 1 at this point, but his injury history is not comforting.

Michael Penix Jr. (left ACL) still hasn’t been cleared for 11-on-11 work in practice, and he told reporters Wednesday he did not have a follow-up appointment scheduled with the surgeon who will sign off on his full participation. Penix, who has a tattered injury history of his own, is improving but trying to remain patient, he said.

“I’m running my own race,” he said. “I just have to take it one day at a time and focus on what I can control. Right now I can’t control not being out there.”

Meanwhile, training camp addition Cooper Rush seems to be slowly nudging out Jack Strand in the rotation, which was expected considering Rush is an eight-year NFL veteran. Rush and Strand split reps with the second team in 11-on-11 work during Saturday night’s practice at Lanier High School.

Overall, the quarterbacks’ results on the practice field are as smooth as you would expect, considering the jumbled rotation, intermittent availability and four quarterbacks learning a new offense. Saturday night, at least, provided some optimism as Tagovailoa was sharp and had nice throws for big gains to Olamide Zaccheaus and Drake London.

Get well (really) soon

The Kansas City Chiefs may be about to start an undrafted rookie free agent, Kahlil Benson, at right tackle. Why does that matter for the Falcons? Because both of Kansas City’s right tackles from the last two years are in Atlanta. The Chiefs allowed Jawaan Taylor to leave via free agency and then traded Wanya Morris to the Falcons in June for a late-round pick swap. That Kansas City didn’t want to hold on to either player is not comforting, given its current state at the position.

The worst part is neither guy is playing right tackle for Atlanta right now. Taylor has not practiced with the team since signing because he is recovering from elbow and triceps injuries suffered last season. Head coach Kevin Stefanski said Taylor is attending all the team’s walkthroughs and meetings and is “close” to returning. Morris, who has missed several days due to a lower-body injury, has worked mostly at left tackle so far, although Stefanski said he will train on both sides.

So who are the Falcons’ right tackles right now? Michael Jerrell, a third-year sixth-round pick with three NFL starts; Brandon Walton, a fourth-year former undrafted free agent with two NFL starts; and Ethan Onianwa, the Falcons’ seventh-round pick this year.

General manager Ian Cunningham and his staff are almost certainly scouting the other 31 training camps for right tackles who might get cut when rosters are trimmed to 53 later this month.

This could be fun

There might be hope we won’t have to watch one of the worst screen games in the NFL this year, so that’ll be nice. Under Stefanski and offensive line coach Bill Callahan, the Falcons seem committed to improving. They are at least putting in the time at practice.

Atlanta is dedicating 10-minute chunks of practice to screens during some practices, left tackle Jake Matthews said.

“Callahan always says, ‘Every screen is different.’ You are never going to get two of the same. It’s really important to practice every type of look you can get,” he said. “You can run the exact same look, and it can play out three different ways.”

The Falcons ranked 26th in the league in EPA per pass play on screens (minus-.25) the last two years, according to TruMedia. It’s not that they didn’t try them. They were 13th in that span with 80 screen completions. They just didn’t work. Atlanta got only 5.8 percent of its passing yards from screens, a mark that ranked 29th in the league.

“The more you get confidence with the guys next to you, those plays can pop and they can be really, really explosive,” Matthews said.

With Bijan Robinson and Zachariah Branch, the Falcons seem well suited to heavy use of screens.

Waiting on the league

I’m worried many Falcons fans aren’t prepared for the length of suspension James Pearce Jr. is going to get. I would expect the league to announce his punishment under the personal conduct policy before rosters are trimmed at the end of this month. It’s going to be at least eight games, in my opinion. Based on the league’s previous rulings in similar situations and the details of Pearce’s February arrest and subsequent three felony charges, I wouldn’t be shocked if it was more.

Atlanta doesn’t appear to be planning on having Pearce early in the season. He has worked mostly with the third team so far, although Saturday night he took some snaps with the first and second units.

The deal maker

I’m good with Cunningham being aggressive on new contracts to lock up the team’s young offensive players. The Robinson and London deals were no-brainers. The Kyle Pitts and Matthew Bergeron contracts can be debated, but Cunningham looks like he got ahead of the market (or at least not behind it) on both deals.

One day after the Falcons made Pitts the third-highest-paid tight end in the league ($18 million), the Jaguars paid Brenton Strange $12 million a year. Strange has 986 receiving yards in three seasons. Less than a week after Atlanta made Bergeron the highest-paid guard in the league ($24 million per year), the Titans topped it with Peter Skoronski’s deal ($25 million per year), continuing a trend of skyrocketing salaries for the position in the last year.

If Pitts and Bergeron don’t perform at the level expected of players making that kind of money, Cunningham will get dinged for it. Right now, these are sensible deals.

The London, Robinson and Pitts contracts have a combined 15 void years tacked on the end, according to OverTheCap.com. The full details of the Bergeron deal aren’t available yet, but it’s likely similar. Void years are essentially extra seasons added to the end of contracts, allowing the salary cap hit to be spread out. Bryce Johnston, Atlanta’s senior vice president of football administration (cap guy), came from Philadelphia, which has used void years liberally to build its roster.

Those void years are one reason Atlanta is projected to have the second-most available salary cap space in the league in 2027 even after all the new deals.

Bright spots at linebacker

Christian Harris is not quite a lock to start at middle linebacker. Rookies Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. each got more time with the starters in practice last week. That may be the coaching staff getting a good look at them before they have to start making depth chart decisions, but it could mean more.

Harris, a third-round pick of the Texans in 2022 who has 27 career starts, is still the favorite to start Week 1 simply because of experience, but it’s good news for Atlanta that the young guys are coming along.

Pads popping

The live tackling at Falcons practices is new, and probably a preview of a change in the preseason plan. Atlanta did not have any live tackling in its training camp practices under previous head coaches Arthur Smith and Raheem Morris, but Stefanski has a different philosophy.

“I think there is a way to work hard and work smart and practice live because that’s what the game is,” he said. “I think there’s a way to do it safely. I think the guys understand how to do that the right way. You’re still not taking a shot on one of your teammates, but like I’ve said before, to get ready to play football, you have to play football.”

Stefanski also plans to play starters in the first and third preseason games, another break from tradition in Atlanta. Penix only threw 16 preseason passes in his rookie year and did not play in the preseason at all last year.

London believes the more physical preseason approach will pay dividends.

“Callousing our body up to go in and play an actual game is really good for us,” the wide receiver said. “I’m excited we’re doing it.”

Cash money

Cash Jones still looks like one of those undrafted free agents who is hard to get rid of. After working with the wide receivers in the spring, he’s at his natural position, running back, this fall.

“Playing running back and wide receiver, what we’re doing there is testing the limits of what he can handle mentally, and he passed all of those,” Stefanski said.

“Cash is smooth,” London said.

Mixing and matching

Especially now that the versatile Jalon Walker is lost for the season, I expect Atlanta’s front seven personnel to be very situationally dependent this year. Every defensive coach would love to have defenders with a varied enough skill set to do everything, but that’s not how this team is built at the moment.

What does that mean? On run downs, I’d expect to see a lot of guys like Cameron Thomas and Bralen Trice at outside linebacker with guys like Da’Shawn Hand and Maason Smith, and a heavy dose of Brandon Dorlus, Samson Ebukam and Azeez Ojulari on passing downs. Smith blew up a red zone play Saturday in what was probably the defensive highlight of the day. (Also, keep an eye on tackle Chris Williams, a former UDFA who had a couple of breakout seasons the last couple of years in Chicago.)

Extra points

Avieon Terrell has some ground to close to earn a starting job in the secondary. With Billy Bowman still on the physically unable to perform list, Darnay Holmes, Sydney Brown and A.J. Woods have all gotten more work as the first-team nickel so far. … It’s notable that Corey Levin appears to be on the first-team field goal unit. Levin has gotten some work at second-team center recently, so his spot on special teams may be a tell. Levin is a six-year vet with a lot of versatility. … I’ve enjoyed seeing DeMarcco Hellams getting some first-team work at safety with Jessie Bates out. Hellams is not a threat to Bates or Xavier Watts, but it’s fun to watch him hit people. … Matt Ryan has filed his retirement paperwork. I checked just to be sure. … It might be time to give up on sixth-round defensive tackle Anterio Thompson being a Falcon this year, or maybe ever. He’s still not with the team due to an issue Stefanski said the team is “working through.”

title: Mahomes, Parsons and trio of 49ers highlight the NFL stars returning from injuries this season
description:
The list of players who finished the 2025 season injured was almost a who's who of some of the NFL's biggest stars.
Most of those other stars are aiming to be back for Week 1, but Parsons will have to wait a little longer.
That was great news for the Chiefs, who managed just one touchdown in three games after Mahomes went down last season.
Now the key is what form will Mahomes be in when he takes the field in Week 1 against Denver.
That never happened as Parsons suffered the knee injury in early December after recording 12 1/2 sacks in 14 games.
text:
The list of players who finished the 2025 season injured was almost a who's who of some of the NFL's biggest stars.

There was two-time MVP and three-time Super Bowl champion Patrick Mahomes, who could only watch the end of a disappointing six-win season for Kansas City after going down with a torn ACL in Week 15.

Three-time All-Pro Micah Parsons was only a spectator in the postseason in his first season in Green Bay after suffering his own torn ACL in December, while the San Francisco 49ers were down three big stars of their own for the end of the playoffs with Fred Warner, Nick Bosa and George Kittle all going out with major injuries during the season.

Indianapolis had its promising season derailed when quarterback Daniel Jones tore his Achilles in early December and the New York Giants missed 2024 rookie sensation Malik Nabers for most of the season after he went down with a knee injury in the fourth game of his second season.

Training camp for those stars has been about getting back up to full strength so they can get back on the field either for the start of the season or at least early on.

"It was always the goal to be able to practice when I got to training camp. We kind of hit that step," Mahomes said at the start of camp. "Now, it's about building and keep getting better and better, so when the regular season comes around, I can be available."

Most of those other stars are aiming to be back for Week 1, but Parsons will have to wait a little longer. He is hoping to return in October and vows the pent-up energy from his time away will only make him better.

"People are worried about the knee. They should be worried about how I'm going to play when I get back," Parsons said. "The anger, the frustration, the things that I'm going to have to let out because of how long it's been since I played."

Here's a look at some of the biggest stars returning from injuries:

PATRICK MAHOMES

When the quarterback Mahomes tore his ACL on Dec. 14 in a loss that eliminated the Chiefs from the playoffs, it was uncertain if he'd be able to make it back in time for Week 1. But he got back on the field for part of the offseason program and was fully cleared for the start of training camp. That was great news for the Chiefs, who managed just one touchdown in three games after Mahomes went down last season.

Now the key is what form will Mahomes be in when he takes the field in Week 1 against Denver. His production has dipped in recent seasons as the talent around him has dropped off. He has also been asked to run more with a career-high 422 rushing yards last season but might need to stay in the pocket more to protect his knee.

MICAH PARSONS

The Packers traded for Parsons before the start of last season to add the defensive superstar who could elevate them in the playoffs. That never happened as Parsons suffered the knee injury in early December after recording 12 1/2 sacks in 14 games.

Green Bay's defense lacks difference-makers and will need a healthy Parsons to make a long playoff run. The team is being cautious in his return and plans to start him on the physically unable to perform list for the regular season. Parsons would have to miss at least four games but said he'd like to be back in time to face his former Dallas Cowboys teammates in Week 6.

SAN FRANCISCO STARS

The 49ers were one of the most injured teams in the league last season with Bosa going down with a season-ending knee injury in Week 3, Warner breaking his ankle in Week 6 and Kittle rupturing his Achilles in a wild-card win at Philadelphia. That trio has seven career All-Pro honors and was a major reason why San Francisco has reached two Super Bowls under Coach Kyle Shanahan.

Warner has been full-go since the start of camp and is ready to return for the opener. Bosa has only taken part in individual drills so far but also is expected back Week 1. Kittle remains on the PUP list and it's uncertain whether he will return on Sept. 11 in Australia against the Los Angeles Rams or shortly after that.

MALIK NABERS

After recording 1,204 receiving yards as a rookie in 2024, the Giants had big hopes last season for Nabers only to see him suffer a season-ending knee injury in Week 4. Nabers' rehab had a few setbacks early but he was able to make it back on the field at the starting of training camp.

New York is relying heavily on Nabers this season to be Jaxson Dart's No. 1 option.

"Every time he's on the field, everybody knows where he's at," Dart said. "There's an aura that he has on the field that is exhilarating. It makes me happy. It makes everybody happy just to see him out there."

DANIEL JONES

Jones had a breakthrough campaign in his first season with the Colts, completing a career-high 68.0% of his passes for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdown passes and only 8 interceptions in 13 games before getting injured.

Indianapolis had one of the most dynamic offenses when Jones was healthy and rewarded him with a two-year deal worth $88 million in the offseason. The Colts are hoping his return will lead to more of the same. Jones managed to make it back on the field to practice on the first day of training camp less than eight months after getting hurt.

Jones has struggled to stay healthy over his career, missing time for injuries almost every season outside of 2022, when he started 16 games for the Giants.

NNAMDI MADUBUIKE

The defensive tackle Madubuike missed most of last season with a neck injury and it was uncertain until this summer if he would ever return. But he came off the PUP list early in camp and appears on track to get back on the field this season for a Baltimore defense that sorely missed him in 2025.

Madubuike made the Pro Bowl in 2023 and '24 with 19 1/2 sacks across those two seasons as one of the game's best interior pass rushers. He had two sacks in the first two games last season before getting shut down with the neck injury.

Baltimore's defense fell off last season in his absence and is looking to get back in form in the first year under new Coach Jesse Minter.

title: Finding the Top 10 Falcons in Bleacher Report's 1000-player NFL Rankings
description:
Who is going to fill those last four as we find the top ten Falcons in Bleacher Report’s 1000-player NFL ranking?
Bijan Robinson, RB, Grade: 94, Rank: 6, Tier: Franchise Cornerstones Bijan Robinson is one of the best running backs in the NFL.
Drake London, WR, Grade: 85, Rank: 71, Tier: Pro-Bowl Caliber Drake London is one of the league’s better young wide receivers.
He has never played with a top-shelf quarterback in the NFL during his career, yet he consistently puts up good numbers.
However, Pearce was a non-factor against the run, and his off-the-field concerns have already surfaced in the NFL.
text:
Before we start this exercise, close your eyes…well, read this first, and then close your eyes. Who are your top ten players for the Atlanta Falcons right now? Obviously, there’s the trio of Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, and Drake London that should be locks, but who else makes the cut? Jessie Bates is a lock as well, but there’s not a lot of room left for some pretty good players that don the red and black right now. Xavier Watts and A.J. Terrell were both recognized as the top 99 defensive players. That’s already six slots looked to be taken up. Who is going to fill those last four as we find the top ten Falcons in Bleacher Report’s 1000-player NFL ranking?

Let us know in the comments if you think Bleacher Report got it right, and if they didn’t, who should be recognized as a top ten Falcon right now.

Bijan Robinson, RB, Grade: 94, Rank: 6, Tier: Franchise Cornerstones

Bijan Robinson is one of the best running backs in the NFL. He is the engine and best player on the Atlanta Falcons offense. Robinson is a natural, elite ball carrier with a strong impact in the passing game as a receiver. He accounted for 2,298 yards from scrimmage and 11 total touchdowns. Robinson is a game-changing player who elevates the offense. His vision, elusiveness, stop/start ability, and burst make him one of the most difficult offensive weapons to defend in the league. Robinson’s pass protection is an issue. He allowed over 10 pressures and three sacks last season. He prefers to lunge or throw a shoulder at incoming defenders. Robinson’s pass-protection technique must improve.

Jessie Bates, S, Grade: 91, Rank: 25, Tier: All-Pro Ability

Jesse Bates sees things before they happen and shows up exactly where he needs to be to make the play. It’s like watching Mysterio fighting Spider-Man, always appearing in places the quarterback doesn’t want him to be and taking the ball away. Bates is one of the prominent ball-hawks in today’s game, and he seamlessly rotates all around the back end, handling a ton of mental responsibilities. He played closer to the line of scrimmage last season than ever before and played fast, took away underneath routes, and helped condense the offense. A continually impressive player continues an impressive career.

Drake London, WR, Grade: 85, Rank: 71, Tier: Pro-Bowl Caliber

Drake London is one of the league’s better young wide receivers. He has never played with a top-shelf quarterback in the NFL during his career, yet he consistently puts up good numbers. He’s held back by that uncertainty with the Falcons quarterback situation. London is an uber-efficient route-runner with strong footwork and use of hands to fend off bump-and-run coverage. He’s the prototypical X-receiver, but he plays all over the formation, forcing advantageous matchups. London isn’t in the elite tier of No. 1 receivers in the league, but with better quarterback play, he will enter the conversation.

Kyle Pitts, TE, Grade: 81, Rank: 112, Tier: High-Quality Starter

Kyle Pitts had some truly lofty expectations to live up to coming out of Florida, and 2025 was an offensive explosion for the fifth-year tight end. He set career highs in targets, receptions, and touchdowns while playing over 200 snaps more than any previous year of his career. Pitts showed growth in nuance in route running, using more speed dilation and deception to get into space while still showcasing his top-tier athletic ability after the catch. He’s a true three-level weapon, and the Falcons use him as such to maximize their passing attack. While Pitts isn’t a game-changer as a run blocker and doesn’t show the effort all the time, his power at the point of attack has improved, and on the move, he can be useful. But he’s out there for one reason: to be a match-up problem.

A.J. Terrell, CB, Grade: 81, Rank: 121, Tier: High-Quality Starter

One of the more underrated corners in the NFL, AJ Terrell is a technician on the outside who forced tight-window throws at the fourth-highest rate in the league last season. He mirrors well, attacks the catch point consistently, and is a willing and able run supporter. Bigger route-runners with a good catch radius take advantage of the space he gives them in off coverage, but he closes and uses leverage well. He doesn’t create a ton of turnovers, but still gets his hands on the football a lot.

Xavier Watts, S, Grade: 81, Rank: 124, Tier: High-Quality Starter

Xavier Watts deserved a stronger push for Defensive Rookie of the Year in 2025. He makes up half of the best safety duo in the league with Jessie Bates, allowed Bates to roam closer to the line of scrimmage, and helped unlock the defense and create turnovers. Watts had five interceptions and 11 passes broken up as a rookie, was a plus run defender from depth, and, while there were some lapses, he showed the ability to recover not just physically but also mentally. He didn’t look like a rookie out there; he handled more rotations, living on top of the defense, and the NFL stage like he was meant to be there.

Chris Lindstrom, G, Grade: 76, Rank: 237, Tier: Critical Roster Piece

Lindstrom remained one of the league’s most durable and dangerous run-blocking guards in 2025, but Atlanta’s schematic shift over the last two seasons made his pass-protection limitations more visible. With the Falcons using far less play-action and exposing the line to more true dropback reps, Lindstrom’s lighter frame and tardier anchor were stressed more often against high-end power. He remains an elite zone run-blocker, winning with rare quickness, leverage, leg drive and strain to reach landmarks, steer defenders and finish at angles most guards cannot access. The contrast is in pass protection, where his profile carries more variance. Lindstrom relies heavily on jump-sets and first meaningful contact to erase rushers’ runway before they can build force, a strategy that is more forgiving off play-action than in static dropback situations. When he lands first, he can still close space and end reps quickly. When he misses or is forced to absorb power late, the losses can be immediate. In the right structure, Lindstrom’s pass protection can play a tier higher, but his current profile is driven by elite run-game value and capped by the volatility of his true pass sets.

Divine Deablo, LB, Grade: 73, Rank: 354, Tier: Reliable Contributor

After flaming out in Las Vegas, Deablo signed with Atlanta last offseason and had a career year. One discernible difference in his play was his instincts against the run, as the former Raider was constantly in the right spot to make tackles for short gains with the Falcons. Also, the college safety finally put it together in coverage on the second level, posting a career high seven passes defended after registering just six in the first four years of his career combined. However, he is still susceptible to the occasional coverage lapse. It will be interesting to see if Deablo can build on a strong campaign and continue to grow in Atlanta.

James Pearce, Jr., EDGE, Grade: 69, Rank: 495, Tier: Functional Performer

Pearce had an impressive rookie campaign as a pass-rusher, notching double-digit sacks with 10.5 in year one. His ability to turn speed to power and use a cross-chop move as a counter keeps offensive tackles on their heels. That, combined with his athleticism and closing speed, gives the Tennessee product a bright future. However, Pearce was a non-factor against the run, and his off-the-field concerns have already surfaced in the NFL.

Jalon Walker, EDGE, Grade: 69, Rank: 504, Tier: Functional Performer

Walker provided plenty of flashes as a pass-rusher during his rookie campaign to suggest he has a bright future, showing off some impressive athleticism and quickness to win around the edge. However, a lot of the 2025 first-round pick’s production came when he was unblocked or via stunts, especially when working against the run. The Georgia product can improve significantly by winning one-on-one opportunities more frequently and making plays on his own. He may have to wait until 2027, however, after suffering an ACL injury during training camp.

Detroit Lions safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch are still on track to return from injury early in the regular season.

Lions coach Dan Campbell said Tuesday, Aug. 11, in Allen Park that Joseph is currently away from the team dealing with a personal issue, but his rehab from last year's season-ending knee injury is "coming along very well."

Joseph, who leads the NFL with 20 interceptions the past four seasons, missed 11 games last season with a chronic knee injury, while Branch is returning from the torn Achilles tendon he suffered last December.

The Lions placed both players on the physically unable to perform list at the start of training camp, and both have worked out sporadically with trainers during training camp practices this summer.

Joseph said July 31 he is "super optimistic" he will return early in the season.

Players can come off PUP anytime during training camp but must miss at least the first four games if they open the regular season on the list.

Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper have taken most of the first-team reps at safety this summer in place of Joseph and Branch.

The Lions open the regular season Sept. 13 against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field in Detroit.

text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Baltimore Ravens starting cornerback Nate Wiggins was carted off the field an hour into Tuesday's practice after suffering a left leg injury.

Wiggins, Baltimore's top cornerback, couldn't put any weight on his left leg when heading into the team facility. He had his arms draped over trainers to go inside.

Ravens coach Jesse Minter declined to give a timetable on Wiggins or specify what he injured.

"I think there's optimism," Minter said after Tuesday's practice. "But we'll look at it [and] we'll see where it's at."

Wiggins, a first-round pick in 2024, was injured during one-on-one drills with rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane. He got his feet tangled with Lane while covering a go route and fell hard to the ground.

Trainers looked at the left leg and knee of Wiggins, who was in visible pain. He is the first player to be carted off in this year's training camp.

"Obviously, Nate is an elite player," Minter said. "I think Nate has potential to be one of the top corners in the whole league. But I feel good about that whole [cornerback] room."

Wiggins is one of the players the Ravens can least afford to lose. The other experienced cornerbacks on the roster are Marlon Humphrey, Chidobe Awuzie and T.J. Tampa.

description:

text:
The Miami Dolphins have the makings of a solid offensive line in place if Kadyn Proctor lives up to expectations and Jonah Savaiinaea can take the anticipated jump in his second season, but there is a clear problem with the group.

That problem is an alarming lack of depth, and it's a concern that's only growing with each passing day.

To help find a potential solution, the Dolphins swung the trade for New England Patriots 2024 third-round pick Caedan Wallace and an ideal world he can live up to his draft status in Miami and provide help either at guard or tackle.

But Wallace has become just one of the many unproven young players in the offensive line room, which continues to be missing the one veteran who projects as the top backup on the unit.

That would free agent acquisition Jamaree Salyer, who has not practiced since the third of training camp back on July 31.

Head coach Jeff Hafley hasn't been asked about Salyer recently, but it's not just that he hasn't practiced, he also hasn't been spotted at practice at all in August — unlike just about everybody else who is dealing with an injury, whether it be Dante Trader Jr., Kevin Coleman Jr., rookie Chris Bell or PUP cornerbacks Storm Duck and Darrell Baker Jr.

This makes it a bit concerning as to Salyer's availability at the start of the regular season. Yes, we're still a month away, but remember that Salyer was carted off the field during minicamp and missed the final week of OTAs.

And the reality is that the Dolphins really can't afford, as presently constituted, to be without Salyer for a long period of time.

Yes, Jamaree Salyer.

THE DOLPHINS' LACK OF DEPTH UP FRONT

Salyer joined the Dolphins as a free agent after spending four seasons with the L.A. Chargers, for whom he played both guard and tackle — and he was very durable there, played all 17 games in 2022-24 before playing 13 last year.

In light of fellow free agent pick-up Charlie Heck's well-publicized struggles in training camp — though he has practiced better the past few days — Salyer looks like he might be the one reliable backup right now at guard or at center.

Andrew Meyer is somebody who showed some promise as a rookie free agent, but the fact remains he's still an unproven commodity.

And the same applies to everybody at tackle outside of Heck.

The newest addition, Wallace, has only 10 games of NFL experience, but that's more than Marques Cox, Kevin Cline and Gottlieb Ayedze combined.

The thought coming out of the spring was that if something were to happen to Austin Jackson — and we don't need to go over his injury history — then Heck simply would fill in, but training camp has provided reason for concern.

Salyer has played right tackle before and right now he would look like a better option. He also would be the top backup at guard, even an option to start if it turned out that Savaiinaea wasn't able to take that step forward after his rough rookie season.

But Salyer has to be healthy and on the field to be able to contribute.

Right now he's not and he hasn't been for more than 10 days, with no clear picture as to when he'll be back.

So, yes, his injury is a clear concern. A major concern.

text:
METAIRIE, La. -- New Orleans Saints defensive end Cameron Jordan could potentially miss the start of the season with a hamstring injury, according to Saints coach Kellen Moore.

Moore said Jordan's injury occurred during Thursday's practice, and he has missed the past three practice sessions. (He was not at Saturday's practice because he attended Drew Brees' Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement.)

Moore said "he's going to miss a little bit of time," but the injury will be reevaluated every few days. Moore didn't initially specify a timeline, but when asked to clarify about the severity, said it could go past the preseason.

"It could possibly get into the season, but you never know," Moore said. "[You need] to have some patience with it, let it take its course and we'll collect more information as we go."

Jordan, 37, has missed only one game due to injury in his career. He missed a Week 11 game during the 2022 season due to an orbital fracture but returned the following week. He also missed one game in 2021 due to COVID-19.

"Let's get to work," Jordan wrote on X on Monday.

The Saints have veterans Chase Young and Carl Granderson on the defensive line and acquired Tyree Wilson via a trade with the Raiders during the draft. They also signed former Patriots defensive end Anfernee Jennings in April.

"We certainly feel good about our depth in that position. We got some really talented players on the edge. We view it as a strength of our football team," Moore said. "We're going to need multiple guys to play throughout the season no matter what. ... So we'll take time to kind of evaluate while Cam's out and see where it looks here through training camp and then these other guys will be ready to go."
